summary: Dividing by 10 or 100 makes every digit ten or a hundred times smaller, so each digit slides one or two places to the RIGHT on a place-value chart while the digits and their order stay the same. 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 (the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 from ones to tenths); 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 (the 4 moves to hundredths and a 0 must hold the empty tenths place). The reliable idea is that digits shift and shrink. 'Add/remove a zero' fails for numbers like 37, which have no trailing zero, and 'move the decimal point' gives the same answer but hides why the values change and can lead to errors when a placeholder is needed.
misconceptions: Applies 'move the decimal point' by rote and gets the magnitude wrong (37 ÷ 10 → 0.37 or 370)
Over-generalises 'divide by 10 = take a zero off', which fails on numbers without a trailing zero

activities.title: Slide the digits right on a place-value chart
steps: Set up a place-value chart with columns labelled hundreds, tens, ones, then a decimal point, then tenths and hundredths.
Place digit cards for 37 (3 in tens, 7 in ones) and predict what dividing by 10 will do.
Divide by 10 by sliding each digit card one column to the RIGHT: the 3 moves from tens to ones, the 7 moves from ones to tenths, giving 3.7. Notice the decimal point itself does not move.
Read the result back by place value: '3 ones and 7 tenths'.
Now place a single digit card for 4 in the ones column and divide by 100 by sliding it two columns right, so the 4 lands in hundredths.
Notice the tenths column is now empty and write a 0 to hold that place, giving 0.04. Say why, without the 0, you would wrongly read 0.4.

Optionally model the same shrink with another representation — base-ten blocks with exchange (letting a flat be one whole so a rod is a tenth of a flat and a small cube a hundredth), a Gattegno tenths/hundredths chart, or a number line — to see the quantity becoming ten or a hundred times smaller.
activities.insight: Dividing by 10 (or 100) shifts every digit one (or two) places right and makes it ten (or a hundred) times smaller; a placeholder zero is needed whenever a column between the point and a digit is left empty.

activities.title: Confront the 'take a zero off' rule
steps: Work out 40 ÷ 10 and notice that 'take a zero off' happens to give 4.
Now try the same rule on 37 ÷ 10 and show it fails — there is no trailing zero to remove, and leaving 37 unchanged (or writing 370) is wrong.
Redo 37 ÷ 10 on the place-value chart by sliding digits right to get 3.7, and state in your own words why the shortcut only worked for 40.

Test 'move the decimal point' similarly and check it against the chart result. Notice that, done correctly, it agrees with the chart, but it does not show that each digit has become ten times smaller.
activities.insight: 'Remove a zero' only works when there is a trailing zero to remove, and 'move the point' gives the right result only when it is applied carefully but does not explain why it works. Sliding each digit one place right and reading place value always works and shows why.

activities.title: Anchor the shrink in money and measurement
steps: Work out £4 ÷ 100 and connect it to 4p, writing it as £0.04; check the 4 sits in the hundredths (pence-of-a-pound) place.
Work out 37 cm ÷ 10 and express the result as 3.7 cm, checking which column each digit lands in.
For each context, say which digit moved and what it is now worth.
activities.insight: Dividing by 10 or 100 means a quantity becomes ten or a hundred times smaller, and the place-value result matches real money and metric amounts.

activities.title: Check placeholder and magnitude with targeted questions
steps: Complete 37 ÷ 10 = ___ and state what each digit is worth.
Choose the correct value of 4 ÷ 100 from 0.4, 0.04, and 0.004, and justify the choice by naming where the 4 lands.
Match each digit in your answers to its place value (ones, tenths, hundredths).
activities.insight: A correct answer must place every digit in the right column, using a placeholder zero where a column is emptied; the 0.4-versus-0.04 distinction is the sharpest test.

activities.title: Static chart as a reference label
steps: Beside the moving chart, keep a labelled still chart and point to where each digit of 37 starts and where it lands after ÷10.
Use it to look up and name the place value of any digit in a result (for example, the hundredths place in 0.04).
activities.insight: A fixed chart names where digits land and supports recall of place-value labels, as a companion to enacting the movement.

checkQuestion: Give the child a place-value chart and say: 'Work out 37 ÷ 10, then 4 ÷ 100. For each answer, tell me what each digit is worth.' Watch how they get the answer — do not tell them a method.
checkAnswer: 37 ÷ 10 = 3.7 (3 ones, 7 tenths); 4 ÷ 100 = 0.04 (4 hundredths, with 0 holding the tenths place). Explains that dividing by 10 shifts every digit one place to the right.
